one_liner: Go hex encode/decode with SSE4.1/AVX assembly; about 19x encoding/hex on encode and 4.6x on decode against current stdlib.
what_it_does: Package hex mirrors the core of Go's encoding/hex (Encode, Decode, EncodeToString, DecodeString, EncodedLen, DecodedLen) and adds EncodeUpper, RawEncode with a caller-supplied 16-byte alphabet, and MustDecodeString. On amd64 with the gc toolchain it dispatches at run time through golang.org/x/sys/cpu to an AVX (VEX-encoded 128-bit) or SSE4.1 kernel, and to Go loops on older CPUs; every other target, gccgo and appengine build hex_other.go, which is the Go-1.7-era stdlib code. It is close to drop-in for byte-slice encoding and decoding, but its error values, partial-result behaviour and streaming API differ from the stdlib.
how_it_is_fast: Encode uses Wojciech Mula's nibble-split technique: per 16 input bytes, PSRLW/PAND split high and low nibbles, PUNPCKLBW/PUNPCKHBW interleave them, and PSHUFB looks each nibble up in the alphabet held in a register, giving 32 output characters with no branches. Decode handles 16 characters per iteration: it lower-cases with OR 0x20, validates all lanes with signed PCMPGTB range checks after an 0x80 bias, folds the result to one PMOVMSKB/TEST branch, converts with PSUBB plus a masked 0x27 correction for letters, and packs nibble pairs with PSHUFB, PSLLW and POR into 8 output bytes. Tails under 16 bytes are handled in-register with PINSR/PEXTR sequences, so nothing reads or writes past the slices.
when_to_use: amd64 services that hex-encode a lot of data (hash digests, IDs, bytea columns, logging of binary blobs): encode stays about 19x the current stdlib at 1 MiB in a 2026 third-party run (18785 vs 980 MB/s).
Bulk hex decoding of trusted or untrusted input on amd64, where it is still about 4.6x the Go 1.19+ table-driven stdlib decoder at 1 MiB (9566 vs 2095 MB/s in the same run).
Inputs from about 32 bytes up; the 2016 README shows 6x encode at 32 B but only 2.08x at 15 B, where call and tail overhead dominate.
Code that needs uppercase output or a custom 16-character alphabet without a second pass (EncodeUpper, RawEncode).
when_not_to_use: arm64 (Graviton, Apple Silicon), ppc64le and other non-amd64 targets: decode falls back to the branchy Go 1.7-era fromHexChar switch, which is slower than Go 1.19+ encoding/hex (go-simd/hex measured about 9.7x slower on arm64), and encode is plain scalar.

Code that relies on stdlib error semantics: odd-length input is rejected before any validation, errors are go-hex's own unexported errLength and InvalidByteError types (errors.Is(err, hex.ErrLength) from encoding/hex never matches), and Decode returns 0 bytes on error while having already written earlier blocks to dst; stdlib returns the count decoded before the error.
Streaming use: there is no NewEncoder/NewDecoder, Dump/Dumper, AppendEncode or AppendDecode; the author's own issue #2 lists the missing upstream changes and it was never done.

New projects that can take a maintained dependency: the repo is archived (2025-09-11) and labelled abandoned, with no go.mod; go-simd/hex is a maintained, error-identical alternative with AVX2 kernels that reports 1.37x faster decode than this package on the same CI run.
AVX2/AVX-512 hardware where you want the last 30%: the 'AVX' path is VEX-encoded 128-bit code, not 256-bit.

integration.dependencies: golang.org/x/sys/cpu (unpinned: the repo has no go.mod)
integration.min_toolchain: Go gc toolchain; Travis tested Go 1.10-1.13; amd64 assembly is Plan 9 syntax with the generator asm_gen.go kept for maintainers only
integration.platforms: amd64 with AVX or SSE4.1 for the SIMD paths (Go fallback below SSE4.1 since 14226a5, 2018-11-01); any other Go target via scalar code
integration.thread_safety: Stateless functions with read-only package tables; safe for concurrent use on distinct buffers (not stated in docs, follows from the code).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial - Encode/Decode/EncodeToString/DecodeString have the same signatures and identical output on valid input, but error types, partial-result counts and odd-length handling differ, and the streaming and Append APIs are missing

gotchas: The README decode ratios (24.83x at 1 KiB, 44.70x at 128 KiB, 37.56x at 128 MiB) were measured on 2016-11-11 against Go 1.7's branchy fromHexChar decoder; Go 1.19 replaced it with a reverseHexTable lookup, and the 2026 third-party run shows only 4.57x. Only the encode gap (stdlib encode is still a scalar table loop) has held up, at about 19x.

In the README the stdlib decode rate falls from about 250 MB/s at 1 KiB and below to 144 MB/s from 16 KiB up while go-hex stays near 6.4 GB/s; this is consistent with the branch predictor memorising the small buffers the benchmark loop repeats (inference, not measured), so the 44x peaks reflect a mispredicting 2016 baseline on random hex.

The decode benchmarks build their input with an overlapping in-place Encode(src, src[:m]). That yields a valid encoding of random bytes only because the amd64 kernel walks backwards in 16-byte blocks; on the Go fallback (non-amd64 or pre-SSE4.1) the forward loop overwrites unread input and produces an all-digit string after the first two characters, so decode numbers reproduced off amd64 time a degenerate, perfectly predictable input.

Panics with 'dst buffer is too small' instead of an index error when dst is short, and DecodeString copies the string to a []byte before decoding; the author tried the stdlib's allocation-saving DecodeString change and saw it benchmark slower (issue #2), so the extra allocation stays.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over seelabs/nasm (AVX2 NASM hex for fixed 256-bit values, aimed at C++/rippled) when you are in Go and need arbitrary-length buffers with validation; within the catalogued Go assembly entries it is the only hex codec. Against the uncatalogued go-simd/hex it wins only on existing adoption (118 known importers on pkg.go.dev, including go-pg, uptrace/bun and Hyperledger Burrow).
verified_claims_summary: The README table (committed 2016-11-11, unknown CPU, GOMAXPROCS 8, Go 1.7 era since sub-benchmarks appear) compares BenchmarkEncode/Decode against BenchmarkRefEncode/RefDecode on encoding/hex with identical setups: encode 2.08x at 15 B to 31.17x at 16 KiB and 10.49x at 128 MiB; decode 4.26x at 14 B to 44.70x at 128 KiB. A 2026 run by the competing go-simd/hex project (1 MiB random buffer, GitHub Actions AMD EPYC, GOAMD64=v1, median of 6) puts it at 18785 vs 980 MB/s encode (19.2x) and 9566 vs 2095 MB/s decode (4.57x) against current encoding/hex.
status_note: Archived 2025-09-11 and labelled abandoned by its author (last code change 2018-11-01, Go fallback for pre-SSE4.1 CPUs), yet BSD-3-Clause (with Wojciech Mula's BSD-2 and the Go Authors' BSD notices), widely imported (118 known importers) and correct on every input byte at every position in its own exhaustive invalid-byte test, so it is safe to keep on amd64 but not worth adopting on arm64.
